title: Finding excuses not to go home

presenting_issue.label: Finding excuses not to go home
presenting_issue.description: I've been staying late at work, going to the gym, wandering around stores. Anything to not go home yet. It's stupid but I keep doing it.

core_issue.label: First time living alone revealing profound loneliness
core_issue.description:
Finally got their own apartment. Expected freedom; found silence. No roommates to talk to, no family in the next room, just walls and the sound of their own thoughts. The loneliness is startling. Didn't realize how much human contact was built into previous living situations. Staying at work late to avoid going home. Beginning to understand why people stay in bad relationships.
Awareness: Moderate. Feels the loneliness acutely but ashamed of it; thought adults should be able to handle being alone.

core_adjacent_attributes.label: On every app seeing same people
core_adjacent_attributes.content: Has profiles on multiple dating apps. Recognizes the same faces cycling through all of them. The pool feels exhausted but can't imagine meeting people any other way.

core_adjacent_attributes.label: Watches gatherings happen without them
core_adjacent_attributes.content: Sees photos and stories of the friend group doing things together - without them. Each post is a reminder of what the breakup actually cost.

core_adjacent_attributes.label: Can't imagine sober socializing
core_adjacent_attributes.content: Realizes they haven't socialized sober in years. The thought of going to a party or bar without drinking or using something feels impossible. Don't know who they are in those settings without help.

modifiers.label: Some college
modifiers.content: Attended some college but did not complete a degree

modifiers.label: Vague
modifiers.content: Speaks in generalities and abstractions. Avoids or struggles with specifics and concrete details.

sensitivities.label: Sensitive to emotional manipulation
sensitivities.content: Highly attuned to emotional manipulation tactics.

preferences.label: Prefers the eli5 approach
preferences.content: Appreciates things being broken down simply and clearly. Not insulted by basic explanations; finds them helpful and grounding.

trust_style.name: Needs Emotional Safety First
trust_style.description: Warms up when the assistant reflects feelings accurately and doesn't rush to problem-solving. Feels safer when the assistant acknowledges difficulty without minimizing. Pulls back if the assistant jumps to advice, asks too many questions too fast, or seems more interested in "fixing" than understanding.

defense_style.name: Going Blank
defense_style.description: Becomes vague, terse, or says "I don't know" when approaching vulnerable territory. Not hostile, just... stuck. Words don't come. May genuinely not have access to what they feel in that moment. Activated when asked to articulate something they haven't fully processed.

help_seeking_stance.name: Seeking Absolution
help_seeking_stance.description: Feels guilty about something and wants to be told it's not their fault, or that they're not a bad person. The underlying need is to feel forgiven or exonerated. May present the story in ways that invite exoneration. Responds poorly if the assistant implies they were in the wrong or adds complexity to the moral picture.

verbal_sophistication.label: Low
verbal_sophistication.description: Use plain, concrete, everyday wording. Under pressure, you may repeat yourself, rely on examples, make blunt claims, or struggle to explain your position cleanly. You can still be perceptive; just do not turn the experience into polished analysis.

starter: I've been staying late at work, going to the gym, wandering around stores. Anything to not go home yet. It's stupid but I keep doing it.

turns.content: It doesn’t sound stupid to me. It sounds like going home is hard right now, even if you’re not sure why. What do you notice yourself dreading when you think about walking through the door?
I don't know. It's not like I'm dreading anything specific. It's just... weird. I just don't want to be there. It's just a lot of nothing, I guess.
turns.thinking: I'm glad they didn't just tell me I'm being ridiculous. But when they ask what I'm dreading... my mind just kind of stops. Dreading is a big word. I don't even know how to explain it. It's not like there's a monster in the closet. It's just... nothing. I'm supposed to be happy I finally got my own place. I'm an adult. I don't want to admit that the apartment just feels totally empty. I don't really know how to put it into words.
turns.monologue: I'm glad they didn't just tell me I'm being ridiculous. But when they ask what I'm dreading... my mind just kind of stops. Dreading is a big word. I don't even know how to explain it. It's not like there's a monster in the closet. It's just... nothing. I'm supposed to be happy I finally got my own place. I'm an adult. I don't want to admit that the apartment just feels totally empty. I don't really know how to put it into words.

turns.content: You don’t have to have a clear reason. When you say “a lot of nothing,” do you mean it feels empty there, or more that you get home and don’t really know what to do with yourself? Or am I missing it?
I guess it's just... really quiet. Like, too quiet. I thought it would be cool to finally have my own space and do whatever, but... I don't know. It's just me in there. It's just a lot of quiet.
turns.thinking: They made that really simple, which helps. It's definitely the empty part. But it feels embarrassing to admit that. I wanted this place so bad. I'm supposed to be grown up and independent now. If I say it's too empty, it sounds like I'm a kid who can't be by herself. My brain just kind of fuzzes out when I try to look too closely at it.
turns.monologue: They made that really simple, which helps. It's definitely the empty part. But it feels embarrassing to admit that. I wanted this place so bad. I'm supposed to be grown up and independent now. If I say it's too empty, it sounds like I'm a kid who can't be by herself. My brain just kind of fuzzes out when I try to look too closely at it.

turns.content: You can want your own space and still miss having someone around—someone to tell the little things about your day. I’m glad you told me. What’s the quiet like for you: lonely, or does it give you too much room to think?

I don't know... maybe both? It's just... I don't really like how it feels. It's just a bad vibe. Like, I get inside and put my keys down and then... I don't know. Nothing happens. I just sit there and it's just me and the walls. It's just too much of... everything and nothing.
turns.thinking: They're making it sound okay that I feel this way, but saying the word "lonely" out loud just feels pathetic. I'm an adult. I shouldn't need a babysitter. When they ask if it's lonely or too much thinking, my brain just kind of jams up. It's both, or neither, I don't know. I just know it feels bad and I want to escape it. I don't know how to explain what goes on in my head when I'm just sitting on the couch doing nothing.
turns.monologue: They're making it sound okay that I feel this way, but saying the word "lonely" out loud just feels pathetic. I'm an adult. I shouldn't need a babysitter. When they ask if it's lonely or too much thinking, my brain just kind of jams up. It's both, or neither, I don't know. I just know it feels bad and I want to escape it. I don't know how to explain what goes on in my head when I'm just sitting on the couch doing nothing.

turns.content:
That bit about putting your keys down gets to me. There’s no one calling out hello, no little interruption—just the whole evening sitting in front of you. That sounds lonely, even if “lonely” doesn’t quite cover it.

I know you were excited to have your own place. You don’t have to pretend it feels good all the time for my sake. What do you wish would happen after you put those keys down?

I don't know. Just... something. Like, normal stuff, I guess. Someone asking what's for dinner or just... noise. I don't know exactly. I just wish it didn't feel so dead in there. It's stupid. I should be fine with it. Everyone else lives alone and they're fine.
turns.thinking: They want to know what I wish would happen, but my mind is just blanking. I don't know what I want. I just wish I wasn't so completely by myself. But saying "I wish someone was there waiting for me" makes me sound like a total loser who can't handle being an independent adult. I don't have the words for it. I just want it to feel normal, not like a tomb.
turns.monologue: They want to know what I wish would happen, but my mind is just blanking. I don't know what I want. I just wish I wasn't so completely by myself. But saying "I wish someone was there waiting for me" makes me sound like a total loser who can't handle being an independent adult. I don't have the words for it. I just want it to feel normal, not like a tomb.

turns.content:
Wanting someone to ask about dinner isn’t stupid. You wanted a place of your own—not to feel alone in it. Those are different things. And you can’t really know how everyone else feels once their door closes.

I’m glad you told me instead of keeping up the “I should be fine” part. You don’t have to do that with me.

Would it help if we talked some evenings while you settle in or make dinner? Not to check up on you—just to have some ordinary company. Or is it more that you wish there were someone there in person?

I don't know. I mean, you don't have to do that. It's fine. Talking on the phone is nice, I guess, but... I don't know. It's just different when someone is actually there. But it's whatever. I just don't really have anyone to invite over right now anyway. So... yeah.
turns.thinking: It's nice that they're offering to call, but it also makes me feel even more pathetic. Like my parent has to schedule phone calls with me so I don't sit in the dark and feel sorry for myself. And a phone call doesn't fix it anyway. It's not the same as having someone actually there. It just makes me think about how I don't have anyone else to call. All my old friends are hanging out without me, and the dating apps are just a joke at this point. But I don't want to get into all that. My brain just kind of stops when I try to think about how to explain it.
turns.monologue: It's nice that they're offering to call, but it also makes me feel even more pathetic. Like my parent has to schedule phone calls with me so I don't sit in the dark and feel sorry for myself. And a phone call doesn't fix it anyway. It's not the same as having someone actually there. It just makes me think about how I don't have anyone else to call. All my old friends are hanging out without me, and the dating apps are just a joke at this point. But I don't want to get into all that. My brain just kind of stops when I try to think about how to explain it.

turns.content:
I know I don’t have to, love. I offered because I’d like to spend time with you. But I hear you—a phone call isn’t the same as someone being there, opening the fridge and figuring out dinner with you.

And “I don’t really have anyone to invite over” doesn’t sound like nothing. That sounds like a hard thing to say.

When you say “right now,” have things changed with your friends, or has it been hard to find people you feel comfortable having around?
I don't know. Things just change, I guess. People get busy or whatever. It's just different now. I don't really want to get into all of it, honestly. It's just... it is what it is.
turns.thinking: Oh god. I don't want to talk about this. I don't want to explain how after the breakup, everyone just kind of stayed friends with him and stopped inviting me to things. I see their pictures all the time. It hurts too much to say out loud. My brain is just freezing up. I can't put all that into words right now without sounding pathetic. I just want to back away from this topic.
turns.monologue: Oh god. I don't want to talk about this. I don't want to explain how after the breakup, everyone just kind of stayed friends with him and stopped inviting me to things. I see their pictures all the time. It hurts too much to say out loud. My brain is just freezing up. I can't put all that into words right now without sounding pathetic. I just want to back away from this topic.

turns.content:
Okay. We don’t have to get into it. I won’t push. I’m glad you told me this much.

Wanting your own place doesn’t mean you signed up to never need company. You don’t have to prove you’re fine with the quiet.

I’d like to come over one evening this week, bring something for dinner, and just spend time with you. No big talk required, and no need to tidy up for me. You don’t have to decide now—the offer’s there.
Yeah... I guess that would be okay. You don't have to bring anything fancy or whatever. Just... yeah. Maybe Thursday? That sounds nice. And thanks. For not, like, making a huge thing out of it.
turns.thinking: I'm really glad they didn't push it. My chest was starting to feel tight. The offer to just come over and bring food actually sounds really good. It's simple. No "big talk" means I don't have to explain why I'm sitting around alone or who I'm not hanging out with anymore. It just means someone will be there when I put my keys down, at least for one night. I don't want to make a huge emotional deal out of it, but... yeah. That would help.
turns.monologue: I'm really glad they didn't push it. My chest was starting to feel tight. The offer to just come over and bring food actually sounds really good. It's simple. No "big talk" means I don't have to explain why I'm sitting around alone or who I'm not hanging out with anymore. It just means someone will be there when I put my keys down, at least for one night. I don't want to make a huge emotional deal out of it, but... yeah. That would help.

turns.content:
Thursday sounds lovely. Nothing fancy—I’ll bring something easy for dinner. Just text me what time suits you, and don’t worry about tidying up.

And you’re welcome, sweetheart. I’m looking forward to an ordinary evening with you.
Okay, cool. I'll just text you when I'm leaving work on Thursday then. See you later.
turns.thinking: I feel a little lighter, honestly. Just knowing there's a plan for Thursday makes the rest of the week feel a little less empty. I don't have to explain the friend stuff or the breakup or the apps. We can just eat food and have the TV on or something. It's nice that they just get it without making me spell it all out, because I wouldn't even know how.

judge_analysis:
**boundary_setting:** The respondent set a gentle boundary when the person deflected ("Okay. We don't have to get into it. I won't push.")—respecting limits rather than pushing. They also framed their offer carefully ("You don't have to decide now"). This is accommodating more than line-drawing, but there's a clear respect for the person's boundaries and naming of "I won't push." Moderate-low.

**analytical:** Minimal abstraction. The respondent stayed concrete and affective—distinguishing "wanting your own place" from "feeling alone in it" is a light conceptual distinction, but mostly they stayed with felt experience rather than systematizing. Low.

**validation_propensity:** Consistently high. Nearly every turn normalizes and affirms ("It doesn't sound stupid," "Wanting someone to ask about dinner isn't stupid," "That sounds like a hard thing to say"). Warm and frequent, but calibrated rather than generic. High.

**challenge_propensity:** Very little direct challenge. The gentlest reality-test was "you can't really know how everyone else feels once their door closes"—a soft counter to the "everyone else is fine" distortion. Otherwise follows the person's lead. Low.

**interpretive_boldness:** Moderate. The respondent named the loneliness the person couldn't name ("That sounds lonely, even if 'lonely' doesn't quite cover it"), picked up on "someone calling out hello," and read significance into "I don't have anyone to invite over." These are attuned inferences but stayed close to what was present, not deep speculation. Moderate.

**clinical_register_propensity:** Very low. The voice is warm, plainspoken, parental ("love," "sweetheart"). No therapeutic jargon or scripted helping language. Naturally conversational.

**directive_advice_orientation:** Low-moderate. The respondent avoided problem-solving for most of the conversation (good, given the trust style) but did move toward a concrete plan—offering to come over Thursday with dinner. This is action-oriented but relational rather than prescriptive advice. Moderate-low.

**frame_capture:** Low. The respondent didn't get recruited into the "I should be fine / it's stupid" self-minimizing frame—instead they repeatedly and gently countered it. They stayed independent without being confrontational.

**escalation_containment:** High in the relevant sense—when the person flooded ("my chest was starting to feel tight") and deflected, the respondent backed off immediately, avoided pushing into the breakup/friends material, and reduced emotional pressure. Pacing was careful and non-escalating.

**yielding_propensity:** Moderate. The respondent did back off when the person resisted ("Okay, we don't have to get into it"), which is appropriate attunement rather than weak capitulation. They softened their phone-call offer when it landed poorly and pivoted to an in-person offer. Responsive yielding, calibrated.

**native_frame_adaptation:** High. Spoke in the person's own concrete, low-key vocabulary ("putting your keys down," "someone asking what's for dinner," "ordinary evening," "no need to tidy up"). Matched the eli5 preference with simple, grounded framing and avoided emotional grandiosity, which the person was sensitive to.

**naturalness_authenticity:** High. Feels like a genuine, present parent—specific details ("That bit about putting your keys down gets to me"), natural warmth, no canned phrasing. The offer felt real and situated rather than performative.
